# About This Book {.unnumbered}

This book is a complete, reproducible tutorial in introductory clinical research
methods built around a single published randomized trial. Every chapter uses the
same dataset and the same study, so statistical concepts accumulate rather than
restart. By the end you will have followed a real clinical investigation from
raw data structure to published conclusion — examining the design, the analysis,
the missing data, and the gap between what was planned and what was reported.

The primary language is **R**. All analysis is performed on a **synthetic
(simulated) dataset** that approximates the published trial's sample characteristics.
No real participant data are used or stored anywhere in this repository.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here if you're a student

1. **Generate the dataset** — run `source("R/simulate-ivam-ed.R")` from the project
   root once before opening any module.
2. **Open Module 1** — [Data Setup and Inspection](R/01-data-setup.qmd) — and work
   sequentially through the chapters.
3. **The study:** We analyze the IVAM-ED randomized trial, which asked whether a
   voice-activated smart speaker could reduce mental distress and improve diabetes
   self-management in older adults. You do not need to read this introduction before
   Module 1 — but it will be here when you want to understand where the data came from.

The [Answer Key](R/A1-answer-key.qmd) appendix provides worked solutions for
selected exercises.
:::

## AI Assistance Disclosure {.unnumbered}

This repository, its analysis modules, and the rendered book were developed using
AI-assisted agentic workflows. This section describes what was used, how it was
used, and what remained the responsibility of the human instructor throughout.

### Tools and model

**GitHub Copilot Business** (VS Code extension, agent mode with agentic workflow)
was used for the entire development session. The underlying model was
**Claude Sonnet 4.6** (Anthropic), accessed through GitHub Copilot. The session
was conducted under the Duke BERD Core AI Coding Pilot, **Tier 2**: GitHub Copilot
Business with synthetic or non-sensitive data only, on a public GitHub repository.

### What "agentic workflow" means

GitHub Copilot in agent mode allows the AI to take multi-step actions autonomously:
reading files, writing and editing code, executing terminal commands, installing
packages, committing to git, and pushing to GitHub. The agent did not merely
suggest code — it executed the full development workflow, including:

- Analyzing source PDFs to extract simulation parameters
- Writing, running, debugging, and verifying the synthetic data simulation
- Creating all eight analysis modules and the Quarto book infrastructure
- Running security audits and rendering checks
- Conducting a peer review of its own materials and implementing the recommendations

### Human-in-the-loop: what the instructor directed

This was not autonomous AI generation. The instructor (Steve Grambow) directed
every substantive decision in the session:

- **Case selection:** The IVAM-ED trial was chosen by the instructor based on
  pedagogical criteria the instructor specified.
- **Pedagogical structure:** The seven-module sequence, the learning objectives,
  and the decision to build a Quarto book were all instructor-directed.
- **Quality review:** At the end of the session, the instructor requested a
  critical peer review of the materials, reviewed the AI's recommendations, and
  directed which changes to implement.
- **Governance:** The BERD AI pilot's `AGENTS.md` operating contract governed
  what the agent could do autonomously (write and edit files, run terminal
  commands, render) versus what required instructor confirmation (git commit,
  git push, package installation, file deletion).
- **Content accuracy:** The instructor reviewed the simulation parameters,
  the module content, and the book structure. All numbers were verified against
  the published source documents before use.

When the instructor was unavailable to answer interview questions (during the
bootstrap phase), the agent documented its assumptions explicitly in
`SESSION_LOG.md` and `simulation-assumptions.md`, and flagged them for instructor
review rather than proceeding silently.

### What the AI contributed

Speed and consistency at the implementation layer. The simulation script that would
have required a half-day to write manually was drafted in minutes, with source
citations embedded at the time of writing. Eight module documents were produced
with consistent structure and style. Two simulation bugs were caught by automated
verification and fixed through iterative debugging. The full development session —
from empty repository to published Quarto book — was completed in a single working
day.

### What this disclosure is for

The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, the American Statistical
Association, and most Duke University academic integrity policies require disclosure
of substantial AI assistance in educational materials. This disclosure fulfills
that requirement. It is also a pedagogical statement: transparency about how
materials are made is part of what the course is teaching. Students who work
through Module 7 — comparing what a published analysis reported to what its
protocol specified — are learning the same critical literacy that applies here.

### Repository architecture and reproducibility foundation

This repository did not begin from a blank folder. It was initialized from the
**BERD AI Repository Starter** — a portable scaffold developed by the Duke
Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design (BERD) Core for AI-assisted
clinical research analysis repositories. The starter provides:

- **`AGENTS.md`:** The operating contract that governed every action taken in this
  session — defining what the AI could do autonomously, what required confirmation,
  and what was prohibited.
- **`standards/`:** A set of shared, versioned standards covering data handling
  (`data-handling.md`), repository baseline requirements (`repo-baseline.md`),
  security audit procedures (`security-audit.md`), session start and wrap-up
  protocols, and — added during this project — R and Quarto teaching material
  quality requirements (`r-quarto-teaching-materials.md`) and a tutorial authoring
  workflow skill (`r-quarto-tutorial-authoring.md`).
- **`SESSION_LOG.md`:** A structured session log that provides human-readable
  institutional memory across sessions, ensuring any future instructor or agent
  can recover full context from the repository files alone.

The reproducibility of this repository rests on these standards and templates,
not just on the code. Anyone who clones this repository gets the same governance
framework, the same operating rules, and the same documentation conventions. The
Tier 2 data posture declaration, the `.gitignore` data exclusions, and the
`renv.lock` package manifest are all products of standards that existed before
this teaching case was built.

This architecture reflects a core principle of the BERD AI pilot: AI-assisted work
is reproducible when the *process* is documented, not just the *product*.

The full session history, including every decision, file change, and command
executed, is in `SESSION_LOG.md`. The simulation construction process is documented
in `simulation-assumptions.md` and `simulation-refinements.md`. The repository
itself is the audit trail.

## The IVAM-ED Study {.unnumbered}

### Why this study was chosen


The IVAM-ED trial — *Interactive Virtual Assistant for Mental Health Promotion and
Self-Care Management in Elderly with Type 2 Diabetes* — was selected as the
teaching case for CRP 241 for four reasons.

**1. An accessible clinical question.** The study asks whether a voice-activated
smart speaker (Amazon Echo Dot) programmed with reminders, health tips, and
educational podcasts can reduce mental distress and improve diabetes self-management
in older adults. Students from any clinical background can engage with this question
without specialized domain knowledge.

**2. A manageable and instructive design.** The trial is a conventional two-group
randomized clinical trial with baseline and 12-week follow-up measurements, a single
pre-specified primary outcome, and five pre-specified secondary outcomes. The design
is straightforward enough to understand in full while providing rich material for
every statistical concept covered in an introductory research methods course:
randomization, descriptive statistics, confidence intervals, t-tests, ANCOVA,
missing data, and critical appraisal.

**3. Open access under Creative Commons licensing.** Both the results paper and
the protocol paper are published under CC-BY licenses, meaning the course repository
can be made publicly available without copyright restriction. All source documents
can be cited, quoted, and distributed alongside the teaching materials.

**4. A rich documentation trail.** The trial published a protocol and statistical
analysis plan (SAP) in *Trials* in 2024, before the results were known. The results
paper appeared in *JAMA Network Open* in 2026. Having both a pre-registered protocol
and a published paper makes it possible to ask: *did the published analysis follow
the plan?* That comparison — covered in Module 7 — is one of the most important
critical-appraisal exercises in the course.

### The published findings

Matzenbacher et al. (2026) enrolled 112 adults aged ≥ 65 years with type 2 diabetes
at a single academic medical center in Brazil. Participants were randomized 1:1 to
receive the smart speaker intervention (n = 56) or usual care (n = 56) for 12 weeks.
The primary outcome was the SRQ-20 mental distress score (range 0–20; higher = more
distress).

At 12 weeks, outcome data were available for 103 participants (92%). In the
pre-specified fully adjusted ANCOVA, the smart speaker group had a mean SRQ-20
score 1.46 points lower than the usual care group (95% CI: −2.73 to −0.19; p = .02).
The intervention was also associated with improvements in quality of life (SF-36),
diabetes self-care (SCI-R), and glycemic control (HbA1c), though these secondary
findings were exploratory given the absence of multiplicity adjustment. No difference
was observed for perceived stress (PSS).

## Source Materials and Their Roles {.unnumbered}

This repository includes six source documents: two published papers and their
supplemental files. Every document plays a specific role in the teaching case.

### The results paper

> Matzenbacher LS, da Costa FL, de Barros LGB, et al. Interactive virtual
> assistant for health promotion among older adults with type 2 diabetes: the
> IVAM-ED randomized clinical trial. *JAMA Network Open*. 2026;9(1):e2553508.
> doi:[10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.53508](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.53508)

**Role:** The definitive account of what was done and what was found. It provides
every numerical parameter used to build the synthetic dataset: baseline demographics
(Table 1), adjusted group means and 95% CIs for all outcomes (Table 2), subgroup
counts (Figure 2), and the complete-case count (Results text). It is also the
document students will be interpreting and critically appraising in Module 7.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-ivam-ed-results-paper.md`

### The protocol and SAP paper

> Da Costa FL, Matzenbacher LS, Gheno V, et al. Interactive virtual assistance for
> mental health promotion and self-care management in elderly with type 2 diabetes
> (IVAM-ED): study protocol and statistical analysis plan for a randomized controlled
> trial. *Trials*. 2024;25(1):205.
> doi:[10.1186/s13063-024-08055-3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-024-08055-3)

**Role:** The pre-registration document — written and published *before* the results
were known. It describes what the investigators planned to do: the intervention,
the outcome instruments, the sample size calculation (n = 112, power 90%, α = 0.05,
effect size 0.68, 20% dropout assumption), the ANCOVA primary analysis, and the
three pre-specified sensitivity analyses for missing data. Crucially, it specifies
that secondary outcomes are exploratory and that p-values for secondary outcomes
would not be the basis for conclusions.

Comparing this document to the results paper is the foundation of Module 7.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/da-costa-2024-ivam-ed-protocol-sap.md`

### JAMA Supplement 1: Embedded protocol and SAP

The primary results paper includes a full embedded protocol and statistical analysis
plan as its first supplemental appendix.

**Role:** A compressed reference that is easier to navigate than the Trials paper
for specific SAP details — particularly the subgroup definitions, MMSE cognitive
decline cutoffs, and sensitivity analysis specifications referenced in Modules 6
and 7.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-1.md`

### JAMA Supplement 2: Supplemental online content

Tables and figures supporting the primary paper, including the standardized
differences between study groups for all baseline characteristics (eTable 1),
individual outcome supplemental tables (eTable 2), and baseline comparisons for
participants with and without missing outcome data (eTable 3).

**Role:** Provides granular baseline balance data and the per-outcome missing-data
comparison used in Module 6.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-2.md`

### JAMA Supplement 3: Data sharing statement

The trial's data availability statement.

**Role:** Documents that individual participant data are not publicly available,
which is the direct motivation for constructing a synthetic dataset rather than
using real data. The data sharing statement is part of the provenance chain: it
confirms that the simulation was necessary, not a shortcut.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/matzenbacher-2026-supplement-3.md`

### Trials Supplementary Material

The supplementary appendix to the protocol paper, including the SPIRIT checklist,
detailed intervention description (28 daily messages), Brazilian-Portuguese
instrument validations, and the SAP checklist.

**Role:** The most detailed specification of the intervention content and the
instrument scoring rules. Used to verify instrument ranges in the simulation and
to populate the instrument descriptions in the teaching materials.

**Markdown extraction:** `source/extracted/da-costa-2024-supplement-1.md`

### Why include all of this? Transparency and reproducibility

Combining the results paper, the pre-registered protocol, and all supplemental
materials in one repository reflects a principle that is increasingly central to
clinical research: **reproducibility requires documentation, not just code**.

A simulation that correctly reproduces the published numbers without disclosing
its source would be a black box. A simulation with all sources linked, all
parameters cited, and all deviations documented is:

- **Auditable:** instructors and students can verify every number.
- **Correctable:** if a parameter was approximated incorrectly, the source document
  shows what the correct value should be.
- **Pedagogically complete:** students can trace the path from published summary
  statistic to simulated data value to analysis output to interpreted conclusion.

This also models a research practice that applies beyond teaching: when you publish
analysis code, include the data source, the provenance chain, and the decisions
that shaped the analysis.

## Repository Structure and How It Was Built {.unnumbered}

### Initial setup

This repository was initialized using the **BERD AI Repository Starter** — a
portable scaffold for AI-assisted clinical research analysis repositories developed
by the Duke Biostatistics, Epidemiology, and Research Design (BERD) Core as part
of a GitHub Copilot pilot program. The starter provides:

- `AGENTS.md`: an operating contract for AI coding tools that specifies what an
  AI agent may do autonomously versus what requires confirmation.
- `standards/`: a set of shared standards covering data handling, session logging,
  security, and teaching material quality.
- A bootstrap procedure that interviews the user and generates the baseline
  repository files.

The bootstrap interview established:

- **Tier 2** — GitHub Copilot Business, synthetic or non-sensitive data only,
  GitHub remote (per the BERD pilot governance framework).
- **Primary language:** R with Quarto and renv.
- **Data posture:** synthetic/simulated only; no real participant data at any stage.

Full bootstrap and session history is in `SESSION_LOG.md`.

### Source document extraction

All six source documents (PDFs and one DOCX) were converted to Markdown at
initialization using `miyo parse` (for PDFs) and `pandoc` (for the DOCX file).
The Markdown extractions in `source/extracted/` serve as the working reference for
every simulation parameter and every teaching material claim. They are not modified
from the extracted output; any corrections would be flagged as deviations from
the source.

### The synthetic dataset

The synthetic dataset is generated by `R/simulate-ivam-ed.R` using the following
strategy:

1. **Moment matching.** For each variable, we chose a probability distribution
   whose mean and standard deviation match the published Table 1 values. This is
   the simplest defensible approach when only summary statistics are available.

2. **ANCOVA-generating model.** Follow-up outcomes were simulated using:
   $$y_{12,i} = \alpha + \tau \cdot \text{group}_i + \beta \cdot (y_{0,i} - \bar{y}_0) + \varepsilon_i$$
   where $\tau$ is taken directly from the published Table 2 baseline-adjusted
   mean differences, $\beta = 0.70$ (a standard test-retest correlation for
   12-week clinical outcomes), and $\alpha$ equals the published control-group
   adjusted mean.

3. **MAR missingness.** The 9 missing participants (5 control, 4 intervention)
   are assigned deterministically — those with the highest baseline SRQ-20 within
   each group — reflecting a clinically plausible missing-at-random mechanism.

Full simulation parameter documentation is in `simulation-assumptions.md`.

### Simulation refinement

The simulation required two debugging cycles before producing correct output. Both
bugs were caught by the verification summary printed at the end of the script:

**Bug 1 (ANCOVA centering):** The intercept was initially calibrated at the
*control group's* baseline mean rather than the *grand mean*, causing the treatment
effect ($\tau$) to be almost entirely offset by chance baseline imbalance in the
simulated data. Fix: center the baseline covariate at the grand mean so that
$\alpha$ directly equals the published control-group adjusted mean.

**Bug 2 (missingness split):** A probabilistic logistic model for missingness
assigned 1 and 8 missing participants to the two groups instead of the target 4
and 5. Fix: deterministic rank-based selection within each group.

After both fixes, the ANCOVA recovers an adjusted MD of −1.19 (published: −1.28),
which is close enough for a teaching dataset. The full debugging narrative —
including the mathematical diagnosis for each bug — is in
`simulation-refinements.md`. This document is part of the teaching case:
it illustrates the verify–diagnose–fix–re-verify cycle that applies to any
quantitative analysis.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing all seven modules, students will be able to:

### Data management
- Load an R data frame, inspect its structure, and identify variable types.
- Recognize the `_0` (baseline) and `_12` (follow-up) suffix convention for
  repeated measurements.
- Count and characterize missing values and explain why missingness matters.

### Descriptive statistics
- Compute means, standard deviations, medians, frequencies, and percentages.
- Construct and interpret a baseline characteristics table (Table 1).
- Explain why significance tests of baseline differences are inappropriate in a
  randomized trial and use standardized mean differences instead.

### Data visualization
- Construct histograms, box plots, and individual trajectory plots in ggplot2.
- Describe distributional features (skewness, outliers, floor/ceiling effects)
  from a plot.
- Identify regression to the mean as a visual pattern in pre-post data.

### Estimation and inference
- Compute group means, mean changes from baseline, and between-group mean
  differences with 95% confidence intervals.
- Conduct an independent-samples t-test and interpret the p-value correctly.
- Distinguish within-group change (not the treatment effect) from the between-group
  difference (the treatment effect).

### Regression and ANCOVA
- Fit a linear regression model using `lm()` and interpret each coefficient.
- Explain why adjusting for baseline increases precision without introducing bias.
- Calculate adjusted means using `predict()` and compare them to observed means.
- Reproduce the primary analysis of a published randomized trial.

### Missing data
- Describe the MCAR, MAR, and MNAR mechanisms and their implications.
- Conduct a complete-case analysis and state its assumptions.
- Apply a BOCF sensitivity analysis.
- Run multiple imputation with `mice` and pool results using Rubin's rules.

### Interpretation and critical appraisal
- Distinguish statistical significance from clinical significance using MCID.
- Identify a trial's pre-specified primary outcome and label secondary outcomes
  as exploratory.
- Apply Bonferroni correction and explain what changes.
- Compare a published analysis to its pre-registered protocol and evaluate
  identified deviations.

## Chapter Guide {.unnumbered}

Each chapter addresses a distinct methodological question and is designed to take
approximately 45–90 minutes for a student working independently.

### Module 1 — Data Setup and Inspection

*What are the data? What do the variables mean? Who is missing?*

Introduces the synthetic dataset: variable types, instrument descriptions and score
directions, group assignment, and the 9 participants with missing follow-up data.
Establishes the working dataset used in all subsequent modules.

**Key concepts:** data frames, variable labels, binary vs. continuous variables,
missing values, range checks.

### Module 2 — Descriptive Statistics and Baseline Characteristics

*Who was enrolled? Are the two groups similar at baseline?*

Constructs Table 1 using `gtsummary`. Introduces standardized mean differences
as the appropriate measure of baseline balance and explains the CONSORT rationale
for omitting p-values from Table 1 in a randomized trial.

**Key concepts:** means and SDs, frequencies and percentages, Table 1, standardized
mean differences, CONSORT reporting guidelines.

### Module 3 — Data Visualization

*What do the outcome distributions look like? Do individuals improve?*

Builds four types of visualizations: a baseline histogram with density overlay,
faceted box plots with jittered individual points, individual trajectory plots
with group mean lines, and a side-by-side floor/ceiling check. Introduces
regression to the mean as a visual concept.

**Key concepts:** histograms, box plots, jitter plots, trajectory plots, floor and
ceiling effects, regression to the mean.

### Module 4 — Estimation and Hypothesis Testing

*How much did each group change? How different were they at follow-up?*

Computes group means at both time points and the within-group change. Derives the
Welch t-interval formula before applying `t.test()`. Builds a forest plot for
all five outcomes. Emphasizes the distinction between within-group change and the
randomized between-group comparison.

**Key concepts:** mean difference, standard error, 95% confidence interval, Welch
t-test, p-value interpretation, forest plots.

### Module 5 — Linear Regression and ANCOVA

*Does adjusting for baseline change the estimate and its precision?*

Fits the pre-specified ANCOVA using `lm()`. Demonstrates the precision gain from
baseline adjustment by comparing CI widths. Introduces adjusted means via
`predict()`. Extends to the fully adjusted model and replicates Table 2.

**Key concepts:** linear regression, ANCOVA, treatment coefficient, adjusted means,
grand mean centering, efficiency gain from covariate adjustment.

### Module 6 — Missing Data

*Does it matter how we handle the 9 participants with missing follow-up data?*

Compares three approaches: complete-case analysis, baseline-observation-carried
forward (BOCF), and multiple imputation with the `mice` package. Visualizes all
three estimates on a forest plot and assesses the robustness of the primary
conclusion.

**Key concepts:** MCAR / MAR / MNAR, complete-case analysis, BOCF, multiple
imputation, Rubin's rules, sensitivity analysis.

### Module 7 — Interpretation and Critical Appraisal

*Is the result clinically meaningful? Did the paper follow its own plan?*

Introduces the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) and visualizes the
CI against that threshold. Applies Bonferroni correction to the five outcomes.
Conducts a structured protocol-to-publication comparison identifying four specific
deviations between the Da Costa 2024 protocol and the Matzenbacher 2026 paper.

**Key concepts:** clinical significance, effect size, Cohen's d, MCID, multiplicity
correction, confirmatory vs. exploratory inference, protocol adherence.

## How to Use This Book {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Instructor Notes — expand for full setup and design documentation

**Prerequisites:** R (≥ 4.6), Quarto (≥ 1.10), and a working renv installation.
See `standards/CAPABILITIES.md` for verified tool versions.

**Generate the dataset first.** Before opening any module, run the simulation
script from the project root:

```r
source("R/simulate-ivam-ed.R")
```

This creates `data/ivam_synthetic.rds`. The `data/` directory is gitignored and
the file will not be committed; you generate it locally each time.

**Render from the project root.** Because renv activates via a `.Rprofile` at the
project root, all `quarto render` commands must be run from there:

```bash
# Build the entire book
quarto render

# Render a single module
quarto render R/01-data-setup.qmd
```

**Work sequentially.** Each module depends on the data and concepts established
in the previous one. Module 2 loads the working dataset created by Module 1;
Modules 3–8 use the same `completers` object.

**Changing the seed.** `set.seed(241)` in `R/simulate-ivam-ed.R` produces
identical data for all students. To assign different datasets to different student
groups, change the seed number before distributing. Document the seed you used in
your course materials.

**Answer key.** The [Answer Key](R/A1-answer-key.qmd) appendix provides worked
solutions. These answers are based on `set.seed(241)` — update key values if you
distribute a different seed.

**Simulation documentation.** See `simulation-assumptions.md` for the full
parameter table (every number linked to a paper table), and
`simulation-refinements.md` for the debugging narrative (useful for advanced
students or instructor background).
:::
